params.prompt: Dennis can avoid a Part D late penalty by enrolling when he is first eligible or keeping drug coverage that is at least as good as Part D. If he goes sixty-three days in a row without that coverage after his initial enrollment period, a penalty can apply. For each full uncovered month, it is one percent of the national base beneficiary premium. He generally pays it as long as he has Part D. People who qualify for Extra Help do not owe this penalty. The Medicare Prescription Payment Plan is separate: it lets members spread their drug costs across the year.

At application the producer delivers the federal buyer’s guide, Choosing a Medigap Policy, and an outline of coverage that summarizes benefits and premiums in a standard format. Maryland gives the applicant thirty days after delivery to return the policy for a full refund, and that right must appear prominently on the first page. If the sale replaces another supplement, a replacement notice is signed, the application asks about existing coverage, and the new insurer must credit the time already served under the old policy, waiving pre-existing condition, waiting, elimination and probationary periods for benefits the old policy covered.

A Maryland supplement must provide at least the federally required minimum benefits, and its deductible and co-insurance benefits must change automatically when Medicare changes, so Dennis never finds a gap opened by a January adjustment. A policy may not duplicate benefits Medicare already pays, may not use exclusions or limitations stricter than Medicare’s, and may not be offered at an unapproved introductory rate. It may not be canceled or nonrenewed except for nonpayment or material misrepresentation, and a spouse’s coverage may not end merely because the insured’s coverage ends. If the insured becomes eligible for Medicaid, benefits and premiums are suspended for up to twenty-four months at the insured’s request.

A Maryland supplement may exclude a pre-existing condition for no more than six months, and may define one no more strictly than a condition for which a physician gave advice or treatment in the six months before coverage. Prior cred-it-able coverage reduces the wait, and replacement eliminates it for covered benefits. Compensation rules protect buyers from churning: a producer’s first-year commission may not exceed two hundred percent of the renewal commission, renewal commissions must continue for a set number of years, and a replacement sale earns only the renewal rate, so there is no bonus for moving Gloria from one supplement to another.

Beyond the federal six-month open enrollment at sixty-five, Maryland adds protections. People under sixty-five who qualify for Medicare because of disability must be offered Plans A and D for six months after Part B enrollment, and the Plan A premium may not exceed the average paid by policyholders sixty-five and older. Since July first, twenty twenty-three, Maryland has a birthday rule: for thirty days after each birthday, an existing policyholder may switch to a policy with equal or lesser benefits from any insurer without underwriting, and insurers must give notice of that right thirty to sixty days before the birthday. Group supplements that end must offer individual conversion, and continuation applies when membership ends.

Gloria wants to know who will pay if she needs to live in a nursing home. First, ask what kind of care she needs. In Original Medicare, Part A can cover up to one hundred days of skilled nursing care in a benefit period if she meets the requirements. That usually includes a hospital stay of at least three days as an inpatient. She shares the cost after day twenty. Help with bathing, dressing or eating alone is different. Medicare generally does not cover that ongoing help. Maryland Medicaid can help if she meets its financial and medical requirements. A private long-term care policy may also pay.

Dennis, sixty-six and working for a large employer, has his group plan primary and Medicare secondary; when he retires, Medicare becomes primary and a supplement fills the gaps. His brother, disabled at fifty-eight and covered through a spouse’s five hundred-employee company, has the group plan primary. Gloria, seventy-one and on Medicare, can use Part A for a qualifying hospital stay and up to one hundred days of skilled nursing care per benefit period. For a year of help with daily activities, she might use long-term care insurance, pay privately, or qualify for Medicaid. Lesson forty-seven builds that policy, and Lesson forty-eight adds Maryland’s rules for it.
